title: Epistolae Et Decreta
author: Vigilius

passages.original: Semper studium fuit orthodoxis et piis imperatoribus patribus nostris, pro tempore exortas hæreses per congregationem religiosissimorum episcoporum amputare, et recta fide sincere prædicata, in pace sanctam Dei Ecclesiam custodire. Quapropter et Constantinus piæ recordationis Ario b blasphemante et dicente, non esse Filium consubstantialem Deo Patri, sed creaturam, et ex non exstantibus factum esse, congregavit Nicææ ex diversis diœcesibus a trecentos decem et octo sanctos Patres : et cum ipse etiam concilio interfuisset, et adjuvisset b eos qui consubstantialem Filium Patri confessi sunt, condemnata Ariana impictatc, studium habuit rectam fidem obtinere.
passages.english: It has always been the endeavour of the orthodox and pious emperors, our fathers, to cut off heresies as they arose from time to time by means of an assembly of most religious bishops, and, the right faith being sincerely preached, to keep the holy Church of God in peace. For this reason Constantine of pious memory too, when Arius was blaspheming and saying that the Son was not consubstantial with God the Father, but a creature, and made out of things that did not exist, gathered at Nicaea from various dioceses three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers; and since he himself was also present at the council and assisted those who confessed the Son consubstantial with the Father, once the Arian impiety had been condemned, he made it his endeavour that the right faith should prevail.
passages.notes: Stray letters 'b' and 'a' are footnote marks and are omitted; 'impictatc' read as 'impietate'.

passages.original: Nam et Vincentio secundae regionis subdiacono, iterum a nobis postea ad Siciliam directo, per eum. filio nostro Pelagio diacono similiter scripsisti : sed quia ita memoratus subdiaconus prospere navigavit, ut illum qui in membrana scripta b portaverat, præcedere potuisset, quantum nobis retulit, ea quæ in membrana scripseras, Pelagius diaconus ipso præ- sente percepit. Ergo dum et te prae omnibus imminente prolatum fuerit judicatum, et tanta in ejus indicati laude succensus per multum tempus scripseris, fecerisve ut nunquam te crederemus ab hac posse rectitudine deviare, immutatum te subito post hæc quadam animi levitate, vulgante opinione comperimus, et cum adversariis Ecclesiæ, qui contra c judicati nostri seriem nitebantur, et a nobis sunt per judicati ipsius tenorem a communione suspensi, secrete tractare : et dum filius noster Paulus diaconus d ad Italiam e discedere voluisset, posteaquam et ad eum pervenit, quod scandalum Ecclesiae in communione adhuc nostra positus, secrete et hic, et in Africana provincia 1, ubi antea defendendo et laudando judicatum nostrum, ejus exemplaria destinastis, facere nitebaris, tunc tibi coepit insistere et dicere, ut si verum esset, prodncere « debuisses;
passages.english: For you also wrote likewise to our son Pelagius the deacon through Vincent, subdeacon of the second region, whom we afterwards sent again to Sicily; but because the said subdeacon sailed so prosperously that he was able to arrive before the man who had carried [your letter] written on parchment, as he reported to us, Pelagius the deacon learned, in his presence, what you had written on the parchment. Therefore, although, when the judgment was issued with you above all pressing [for it], you were so fired in praise of that judgment that you wrote for a long time, and acted so that we believed you could never stray from this rectitude, we learned through common report that after this you had suddenly changed through a certain fickleness of mind, and were negotiating secretly with the adversaries of the Church who were striving against the course of our judgment and who had been suspended by us from communion according to the tenor of that same judgment. And when our son Paul the deacon wished to depart for Italy, after it came to his knowledge that, while still placed in our communion, you were striving to cause a scandal to the Church secretly both here and in the province of Africa, where earlier, by defending and praising our judgment, you had sent copies of it, he then began to press you and to say that, if it were true, you ought to bring it forward;
passages.notes: The construction of 'dum et te prae omnibus imminente prolatum fuerit judicatum' is awkward and possibly corrupt ('te imminente' read as 'with you pressing'); 'indicati' read as 'judicati', 'prodncere' as 'producere'. 'producere' ('bring forward/disclose') is uncertain in sense. Stray letters (b, c, d, e, 1, «) omitted.

passages.original: In supradicto decimo septimo capitulo ex verbis B. Petri, quibus in Actis apostolorum dicit: Baptizetur unusquisque vestrum in nomine Jesu Christi, hoc astruitur, quia in ea invocatione, quæ in nomine Palris et Filii et Spiritus sancti fit, non contineatur et Christus et quod dixit Petrus apostolus, debere eos in Christi nomine baptizari, ut secundum hunc intellectum appareat introducta quaternitas. Adjicitur etiam in eodem capitulo, quia sic a Christo Christiani vocemur, quemadmodum diversarum sectarum et errorum sequaces ab inventoribus et magistris suis sunt sortiti vocabula, ut a Platone Platonici, a Marcione Mar- cionistac, et a Manichæo [Manete] Manichaei. Si quis haec ita sapit, docet, credit aut praedicat, anathema sit. Nos enim ideo Christiani vocamur et sumus, quia ipsumDominumnostrum Jesuin Christum in baptisma percipientes induimus, ipso nobis existente capite omnes in eodem unum corpus efficimur.
passages.english: In the aforesaid seventeenth chapter, from the words of blessed Peter, in which he says in the Acts of the Apostles, "Let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ," this is asserted: that in the invocation which is made in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit Christ is not also contained, and [that] what the apostle Peter said, that they ought to be baptized in the name of Christ, [means] that according to this understanding a quaternity would appear to be introduced. It is also added in the same chapter that we are called Christians from Christ in the same way as the followers of various sects and errors have received their names from their founders and teachers, as Platonists from Plato, Marcionists from Marcion, and Manichaeans from Manichaeus [Mani]. If anyone thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things so, let him be anathema. For we are called Christians, and are [Christians], for this reason: that receiving our Lord Jesus Christ himself in baptism we have put him on, and, with him being our head, we all are made one body in him.
passages.notes: "[Manete]" is the edition's bracketed addition, rendered as [Mani].

passages.original: Dispensatim vero mentionem viri non fecit, neque eum nominatim anathemati subdidit, neque alios. Ipsam vero synodum Ephesinam primam sollicite recensentes, nihil de Theodori Mopsuesteni persona referre comperimus, sed symbolum, quod Charisius presbyter illic prodidit, magis quia ab Athanasio et Photio, qui tunc temporis hæretico Nestorio adhaerebant, per Antonium et Jacobum nomina tantum presbyterorum habentes ad Philadelphiorum ecclesias fuerit destinatum : ex quo claret beatum Cyrillum hoc quod per litteras profitetur a prolatoribus scilicet symboli jam defuncti Theodori episcopi nomen fuisse delatum, sua providentia ecclesiasticam moderationem circa mortuum sapientia sacerdotali servantem, noluisse nomen ejus, ne monumentis quidem synodalibus, propter regulam quae de mortuis in sacerdotio servanda est, contineri.
passages.english: But by way of dispensation he made no mention of the man, nor did he subject him by name to anathema, nor others. And carefully reviewing the first synod of Ephesus itself, we find that it records nothing about the person of Theodore of Mopsuestia, but [only] the creed which the presbyter Charisius produced there, chiefly because it had been sent to the churches of the Philadelphians by Athanasius and Photius, who at that time adhered to the heretic Nestorius, through Antonius and Jacobus, who held only the title of presbyters. From this it is clear that blessed Cyril, in what he declares in his letter, namely that the name of the already deceased bishop Theodore was brought forward by those who produced the creed, preserving by his foresight and priestly wisdom the Church's moderation toward a dead man, did not wish his name to be contained even in the synodal records, because of the rule that is to be observed in the priesthood concerning the dead.
passages.notes: The syntax of the last sentence is loose; the sense is rendered.

passages.original: Nam et venerabilis memoriæ Juvenalis interlocutio hoc idem significat : quod Ibas episcopus de eo quod sancto Cyrillo capitula ejus aliter intelligendo detra- xerat, postea professus, quia, his ab eo explanatis et a se intellectis, in communionem eius devote concur.
passages.english: For the intervention of Juvenal of venerable memory also signifies the same thing: that bishop Ibas, concerning the fact that he had disparaged Saint Cyril's chapters by understanding them otherwise, afterwards declared that, once these had been explained by him and understood by himself, he devoutly joined in communion with him.
passages.notes: The sentence breaks off at "concur-"; the verb (concurrerit/concurrisset) is completed from the following context "-rerit".

passages.original: Similiter hoc quoque ausus est dicere, quod confessionem quam Thomas edidit, attrectans manus et latus Domini post resurrectionem, dicens : Dominus meus et Deut meus, non ad Christum retulit (neque enim Theodorus ait Christum esse Deum); sed propter miracula resurrectionis stupentem Thomam laudasso Deum, eaque verba dixisse. Quod autem pcjus est, in interpretatione quam scilicet ad apostolorum Acta idem Theodorus scripsit, similem fecit Christum Platoni, et Manichæo, et Epicuro, et Marcioni, dicens : Quoniam sicut illorum singuli ex proprio dogmate cujus auctores fuerunt, suos discipulos appellavere Platonicos, et Ala nichæos, et Epicureos, atque Marcionistas, eodem modo Christus dogma inveniens, ea eo Christianos appellavit.
passages.english: Likewise he also dared to say that the confession which Thomas made when touching the hands and side of the Lord after the resurrection, saying, 'My Lord and my God', he did not refer to Christ (for Theodore does not say that Christ is God), but that Thomas, astonished by the miracles of the resurrection, praised God and spoke those words. And what is worse, in the commentary which this same Theodore wrote on the Acts of the Apostles, he made Christ like Plato, Mani, Epicurus and Marcion, saying: 'Just as each of them, from the particular doctrine of which they were the authors, called their disciples Platonists, Manichaeans, Epicureans and Marcionites, in the same way Christ, having devised a doctrine, called [his disciples] Christians from it.'
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'Deut' for 'Deus', 'laudasso' for 'laudasse', 'pcjus' for 'pejus', 'Ala nichæos' for 'Manichaeos', 'ea eo' for 'ex eo'.

passages.original: Antequam vero quid egerit in hae causa explicem, observandum est cum Pelagio et B. Gregorio, in hac controversia non disputatum fuisse de fide, sed de Personis. Id testatur Pelagius I in epistola ad Childebertum regem Francorum, qui tunc iri Oriente capitula quædam extra fidem agitata fuisse scribit. B. iboque Gregorius Hiberniæ episcopos monet, in ea synodo de quibusdam solummodo personis actitatum;
passages.english: Before I explain what he did in this case, it should be observed, with Pelagius and Blessed Gregory, that in this controversy the dispute was not about the faith but about persons. Pelagius I testifies to this in his letter to Childebert, king of the Franks, writing that certain chapters were then being debated in the East outside [matters of] the faith. And therefore Blessed Gregory advises the bishops of Ireland that in that synod the proceedings concerned only certain persons;

passages.original: Quippe prima regula quæ in constituto figitur, hæc est : Nihil ex iis quæ quoquomodo disposita sunt in concilio Chalcedonensi, posse in quæstionem deduci, seu retractari, cujus reguhe probatio petitur ex epistolis Lconis papæ ad Leonem imperatorem, et ex epistolis Simplicii ad Zenonem. Econtrario Pelagius docet (Cap. 17, 18) solam fidei causam, quæ definita est in concilio Chalcedonensi, irretractabilem esse: caetera vero omnia, quæ discussa sunt in illa synodo, ad privata negotia pertinere. Leonis testimonia interpretatur (Cap.
passages.english: For the first rule laid down in the Constitutum is this: that nothing of what was in any way settled at the council of Chalcedon can be brought into question or reconsidered; and proof of this rule is sought from the letters of Pope Leo to the emperor Leo and from the letters of Simplicius to Zeno. On the contrary, Pelagius teaches (chapters 17, 18) that only the cause of the faith which was defined at the council of Chalcedon is not to be reconsidered, but that everything else discussed at that synod belongs to private business. He interprets the testimonies of Leo (chapter
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-reference; the chapter number (19) follows in the next section.

passages.original: Secunda regula juxta constitulum hæc est, eos qui in communione et pace Ecclesiæ moroni sunt, post obitum non posse subjici anathemati. Quam regulam confirmat Vigilius allatis Leonis et Gelasti testimoniis. Unde sequebatur Theodorum post mortem damnari non posse. Pelagius vero docet ex Augustino, post mortem quoque eos recte damuari, qui hæresim professi sunt, cum culpa in fide perpetrata nec morte interveniente laxetur. Nempe ad exemplum perduellionis reorum, quorum memoria post mortem damnatur, et bona aldicuntur fisco, licet omnia crimina mortalitate exstinguantur, ut loquitur Papinianus.
passages.english: The second rule according to the Constitutum is this: that those who have died in the communion and peace of the Church cannot be subjected to anathema after death. Vigilius confirms this rule by adducing testimonies of Leo and Gelasius. From this it followed that Theodore could not be condemned after death. Pelagius, however, teaches from Augustine that those who professed heresy are rightly condemned even after death, since a fault committed in matters of faith is not remitted even by the intervention of death. Indeed [this is] after the example of those accused of treason, whose memory is condemned after death and whose goods are adjudged to the treasury, although all crimes are extinguished by death, as Papinian puts it.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: constitulum = constitutum, moroni = mortui, Gelasti = Gelasii, damuari = damnari, aldicuntur = addicuntur.

passages.original: Ex antiquitate vero Latinae interpretationis ducere oportet, cur in actis nostris omissa sit illa damnatio, quæ hoc ordine decreta est. Justinianus interim, dum Vigilius deliberat an cedere vel contendere malit ob tria capitula, edicto suo synodum interpellavit, ut Origenis sectarios anathemate confoderet. Aditus fuerat princeps libello sibi oblato, ab Eulogio, Conone, Cyriaco et Pancratio mnnachis, qui conquerebantur aliquos esse mouachos Hierosolymis, qui impios Origenis errores profiterentur.
passages.english: But it is from the antiquity of the Latin translation that one must derive why that condemnation, which was decreed in this order, has been omitted in our acts. Meanwhile Justinian, while Vigilius was deliberating whether he preferred to yield or to contend over the Three Chapters, addressed the synod by his edict, [asking] that it should pierce the followers of Origen with anathema. The emperor had been approached by a petition presented to him by the monks Eulogius, Conon, Cyriacus and Pancratius, who complained that there were some monks at Jerusalem who professed the impious errors of Origen.
passages.notes: "Aditus" read as "Aditus fuerat" = had been approached; "mnnachis/mouachos" = monachis/monachos.

passages.original: Idem judicium misso edicto suo, a Vigilio papa ct ab aliis patriarchis expetivit et impetravit. Quod testatur Liberatus his verbis (Breviarii c. 23) : Jubente eo (Justiniano, qui mollis loquitur; non enim asurpat jubendi verbum, sed hortandi προτρήπομεν ; inquit) dicta est in Origenem, et illa capitula, anathematis damnatio, quam subscribentes una cum Menna archiepiscopo apud Constantinopolim reperti. Deinde directa est Vigilio Romano episcopo, Zoilo Alexandrino, Euphremio Antiocheno, et Petro Hierosolymitano.
passages.english: He sought and obtained the same judgement, by sending his edict, from Pope Vigilius and from the other patriarchs. Liberatus attests this in these words (Breviarium ch. 23): "At his command (Justinian's, who speaks more gently; for he does not use the verb of commanding but of exhorting, 'we urge', he says) a condemnation of anathema was pronounced against Origen and those chapters, which those found at Constantinople signed together with archbishop Menas. Then it was sent to Vigilius, bishop of Rome, Zoilus of Alexandria, Ephraim of Antioch, and Peter of Jerusalem."
passages.notes: "mollis" read as "mollius"; "asurpat" = usurpat. The Greek προτρέπομεν (misprinted προτρήπομεν) means "we urge". "Euphremio" is presumably Ephraim of Antioch.
